facts.fact: A Vietnamese shop article names the term "Màng sinh học (Biofilm)".
The same Vietnamese article also writes "lớp màng sinh học" and "lớp biofilm dày đặc" for the film.
Vietnamese shop pages write the term as "màng vi sinh (biofirm)", spelled that way on the page.
Biofilm is a thin layer of microorganisms (bacteria, microalgae, fungi, protozoa) held together by a sticky matrix that they produce.
In a mature tank, biofilm coats nearly every submerged surface.
The microbes in biofilm make a clear slime called glycocalyx, which helps them hold onto surfaces.
Biofilm does not need light to grow, only nutrients in the water.
The bacteria and fungi in biofilm on wood can help break down waste.
At normal levels biofilm is too thin to see; you may only feel a slight sliminess on the inside of the glass.
A thick layer of biofilm looks like clear or cloudy jelly.
On new driftwood, biofilm shows as a white or grey fuzzy layer.
Biofilm on wood looks like whitish, cloudy or stringy slime, sometimes a slimy white or clear fuzz.
Biofilm grows on glass, driftwood, lava rock, cholla wood, sponge filter media and moss.
Biofilm also grows on leaves, plants and substrate, and can form an oily layer on the water surface.
Green growth is algae, not biofilm; brown growth may be diatoms or biofilm that contains diatoms.
Biofilm differs from a bacterial bloom: a bloom makes the water itself cloudy, while biofilm sits on surfaces.
Blue-green cyanobacteria form slimy, foul-smelling sheets on the substrate and should not be mistaken for biofilm.
New wood gives biofilm nutrients, so the film often appears after driftwood is added.
A white, slimy film can appear a few days to a week after new driftwood goes in, as organic matter left in the wood ferments.
The white film on new driftwood is a harmless bacterial biofilm that usually clears in 2 to 6 weeks.
Biofilm on aquarium wood is safe and natural, and usually fades within a few weeks as the tank matures and the wood's nutrients run out.
The white film on new driftwood is not toxic, and shrimp usually clean it off within a few days.
Extra biofilm on wood is mostly cosmetic, but it can cloud the water slightly when disturbed and can smother mosses or plants attached to the wood.

Animals that eat biofilm on wood include Amano, Cherry and Crystal Red shrimp, Otocinclus catfish, small plecos such as Bristlenose, and Nerite and Clithon snails; Guppies and Endlers may nibble at it.
Shrimp, fish fry and Otocinclus catfish graze biofilm; baby shrimp rely almost entirely on it in their first weeks.
Young ornamental shrimp spend much of their time on driftwood grazing the biofilm; Nerita snails also eat the white film.
Shrimp graze biofilm all day, and tanks with plenty of it tend to have the best breeding success; if biofilm is scarce, other food may be needed.
Biofilm is a continuous, nutritionally complete food, and shrimp pellets should only be a supplement offered 2 to 3 times weekly.
To grow more biofilm, feed more often (but not so much that food rots) and use powdered foods spread by filter flow.
Leaf litter and alder cones, hardscape such as driftwood, cholla wood or lava rock, and moss or the roots of floating plants like Salvinia all help biofilm grow.
Biofilm takes a few days to start and a few weeks to build up.
In most cases, leave biofilm on wood alone; remove loose bits with a turkey baster or siphon, or gently scrub the wood in tank water and then change some water.
A common mistake is scrubbing every surface during maintenance; cleaning only the front glass is enough.
Scrubbing the white film off new wood is unnecessary because it will come back.
Overdosing biofilm supplements such as Bacter AE can temporarily lower dissolved oxygen, especially in small, warm tanks.
Adding shrimp before the tank has matured is a mistake; maturing takes 6 to 8 weeks.
Adding a biofilm-eating cleanup crew before the tank has cycled is a mistake.
Overfeeding or overdosing powdered food to grow biofilm raises ammonia, nitrite and nitrate and can invite Planaria.
Too much biofilm can use up oxygen, leaving shrimp gasping at the surface.
Shrimpscience says the belief that lots of biofilm means the tank is cycled is wrong; test the water before adding shrimp.
Shrimpscience says biofilm and algae are not the same thing.
Shrimpscience says the belief that biofilm needs light is wrong; it only needs nutrients.
Shrimpscience says it is a myth that biofilm is always visible; at normal levels you cannot see it.
Surface film is a hazy, sometimes rainbow-sheened biofilm made mainly of proteins, oils and bacteria where the water meets the air.
Causes of surface film include uneaten food, still water, bacteria at the surface (especially in new tanks), decaying plants and skin oils from hands.
Surface film also comes from weak surface movement, a filter outlet aimed too low, clogged filter sponges, oily or excess food, organic waste, covered tanks and recent medicines or additives.
Thick surface film slows gas exchange and can lower dissolved oxygen; fish gasping at the surface may be a sign.
Surface film that blocks gas exchange can raise CO2, lower pH in low-buffer tanks and crash the cycle.
Thick surface film can scatter the light that reaches plants.
If fish gasp under surface film, increase aeration at once and check ammonia and nitrite.
To remove surface film, lay an unscented paper towel on the water and lift it off; this is quick but temporary.
Surface film can also be siphoned off with airline tubing during water changes.
Angle the filter outlet so it ripples the surface gently, without violent splashing.
In planted CO2 tanks, run an air stone only at night.
A surface skimmer is the most effective lasting fix for surface film.
Clear uneaten food within 2-3 minutes, remove dead leaves, and rinse your hands before reaching into the tank.
Repeatedly scooping off surface film without fixing flow and waste, or adding random chemicals, is a mistake.
In warm tanks at 28-32°C, oxygen is already lower, so surface film matters more (said for Singapore's similar tropical climate).
Lũa Cholla: the fibers of cholla wood give biofilm more surface to grow on, and young shrimp especially like to eat it.
Lũa Cholla Lớn is sold with the English name "Cholla Cactus"; shrimp may also eat its fibers as roughage.
Lũa cholla (English "cholla cactus") is the leftover hollow, honeycomb-holed skeleton of a dead cholla cactus; it is light but strong.
Lũa cholla may float for 1 to 3 days when new; weigh it down with a stone or fix it to the glass with a suction cup.
Lũa Cholla Lớn sinks on its own after about 1 to 2 days in the tank.
Lũa cholla releases tannins and is acidic, so it can lower pH and soften the water; the page says it does not discolor the water.
Lũa Cholla preparation: brush off dirt without soap or chemicals, boil 30–45 minutes, then soak 1–2 days in clean water until it sinks.
Lũa Cholla Lớn: boil on low heat for about 30 minutes before use; soaking also works but takes about 3 to 4 days longer.
Lũa cholla: boil for at least 4 to 5 minutes before use to remove pathogens and dust.
Lũa cholla: boiling disinfects it but makes the wood break down much faster.
Lũa cholla decays slowly: small pieces last about 7 to 14 months and large ones years, and the decay does not harm shrimp.
Lũa Cholla: putting dry, untreated wood straight into the tank can dirty the water and bring in insect eggs or fungal spores.
Lũa Cholla that still floats after soaking can be boiled again for about 15–20 minutes and weighed down for a few days.

During routine water changes, a gravel vacuum can be used to siphon biofilm directly off the wood surface; a turkey baster can also blast it off the wood while it stays in the tank, and the filter then collects the loosened bits.
First patches of white growth appear about days 2 to 5 after new driftwood goes in, usually starting in crevices and rough areas of the wood.
JUWEL says the suction of its EccoSkim surface skimmer quickly removes residue film and other organic residues from the water surface.
JUWEL says removing residue film and dirt from the water surface raises the oxygen content, helping plants and fish thrive.
A thick film on the water surface reduces gas exchange, which over time lowers the dissolved oxygen in the tank.
A hang-on surface skimmer keeps pulling the top layer of water through a fine filter, removing protein film entirely; FishyHub calls it the permanent solution.
Too much oily film on the surface can stop oxygen from entering the water and harm the tank's animals.
A surface skimmer is made to remove oily film from the water surface and also works to stop the film from forming.
